narratives.narrative: Set inside a psalm that contrasts two interiors, this reading catches the righteous man precisely at his open hand: 'the righteous is generous and gives' (101 sense). It is classed not as feeling but as volition (102 type) — an act of the will, chosen giving, not a mood. The bearer is the righteous man himself (105), and the operation names the contrast directly: the wicked borrows and does not repay, but the righteous is generous and gives, open-handedness read as a mark of the righteous interior (106). Its target is generosity itself (107) and its coupling is the welded pair generous-and-gives (112) — disposition and deed fused so that the giving is the generosity, not a separate consequence of it. The discovery (114) sharpens the point: the righteous interior is marked by a freedom to give that the grasping wicked lacks. Read as a characteristic (115), it is located wholly within the man as an interior state (116 internal:ib-state). The silences are telling and must be read: no seat is recorded (104 none) — the generosity is not lodged in any bodily organ, it is simply a state of the whole man; no manner is given (108 none) — the text does not colour how he gives, only that he does; and source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent — scripture does not trace where this open-handedness rises from, does not grade it, does not narrow it, records no downstream result, and does not fence it as forbidden. What is left is bare and clean: the will to give, welded to the giving, standing as the visible signature of a righteous inner life against the closed fist of the wicked.
narratives.story: In a psalm that holds two kinds of people side by side, this moment catches the good man with his hand open: he is generous and he gives. It is not a passing feeling but a settled choice of the will. The wicked man in the same lines borrows and never pays back, always grasping; the righteous man simply gives, and the giving is the generosity — the two are one thing. The text does not say what part of him this comes from, how strongly he feels it, or what it leads to next; it does not even say where inside him it lives, only that it is the whole man. What stands out, plainly, is a freedom to give that the tight-fisted never have — and that freedom is the mark of a good inner life.

narratives.narrative: In the royal wedding song this reading finds grace not as a deed but as a bearing: 'grace (chen) is poured upon your lips' (101 sense) — favour, charm, the winsomeness of the king's speech. It is classed as status (102 type), a standing quality of the person rather than an action performed, and this classification governs the whole reading. The bearer is the king (105). Strikingly, the two verbs of process go silent: operation is none (106) and target is none (107) — grace here does not move out toward anyone or do anything; it rests on him as an attribute. What is recorded instead is its manner: poured on his lips (108) — the one positive descriptor, locating the grace in his gracious, winsome speech. The coupling ties it to consequence — the graciousness for which God blessed him (112, a spanned pair) — yet the blessing is read as the qualifier, not the characteristic itself. The discovery (114) confirms the gracious character expressed in his words. It is a characteristic (115), an interior state (116 internal:ib-state). The absences carry weight: no seat (104 none) — the charm is not organ-lodged; and with operation and target both 'none', grace here is emphatically not an outgoing act of mercy but a possessed quality, a winsomeness that simply adorns the man. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent — no origin, degree, narrowing, result or fence is given. The finding is that within this family grace can appear as sheer attractive standing, favour resting on a person, before it is ever a thing done to another.
narratives.story: In this royal wedding poem, grace is not something the king does but something he carries: a charm and winning favour that rests on his very words — grace is 'poured upon his lips.' It is a quality he has, a bearing, not an act reaching out to anyone. Notice what the poem does not say: this grace goes out to no one and accomplishes nothing here; it simply adorns him, and God has blessed him for it. It sits in no single part of him, has no measured strength, and leads to nothing further that is named. What we are left with is grace as pure attractiveness — favour and charm resting on a man — before it is ever a kindness shown to someone else.

narratives.narrative: Here mercy is not shown but sought: the psalmist begs God, 'hide not yourself from my plea for mercy' — a plea for grace, a supplication (101 sense, techinnah). It is classed as action (102 type): this mercy-word names the humbled cry itself, a thing the interior does. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to plead for favour (106); the target is God (107). The coupling is telling — twinned with the prayer (112, a spanned pair): the plea for mercy and the prayer are bound together, the supplication the inner posture beneath the outward prayer. The discovery (114) reads it exactly so: techinnah is the humbled cry that expects nothing by right, only mercy — the posture beneath the prayer. Its locus is external:god (116): unlike the possessed graciousness of the king, this movement reaches outside the self toward God as its whole horizon. The silences frame the humbling: no seat (104 none) — the plea is not lodged in an organ but is the man's whole reaching; no manner (108 none) — the cry is not otherwise coloured; and source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no origin, degree, narrowing, outcome or fence is set down. Surrounded in the passage by moaning, anguish, terror and trembling, the mercy here is the interior turned upward in dependence: not a quality it holds but a favour it has none of by right and must beg.
narratives.story: In this reading mercy is not something given but something desperately asked for. The psalmist, surrounded by dread and inner anguish, cries to God: do not hide from my plea. This plea is the very heart of his prayer — a humbled cry that claims nothing as owed and asks only for undeserved kindness. It is aimed entirely at God, reaching out beyond himself. The text does not say where in him it starts, how loud it is, or what it achieves; it simply shows a person in trouble turning upward, empty-handed, and begging for grace he cannot demand. Where grace can be a charm a man possesses, here it is a favour he lacks and must ask for.

narratives.narrative: In the psalm of the ideal king, pity is the inward face of just rule: 'he has pity (chus) on the weak and the needy' (101 sense). It is classed as status (102 type) — a settled quality of the king's person, kingship marked by pity rather than a single passing act. The bearer is the king (105); the operation is to have pity or compassion (106). Two spanned pairs give the reading its shape: the target is the weak and needy (107, spanned), and the coupling binds the pity to saving their lives (112, spanned) — so the compassion is not a mere feeling but is welded to rescue, the inward mercy behind the king's saving acts. The discovery (114) names it as the tenderness of the just king, the compassion that spares and cares for the weak, kingship marked by pity, not merely power. It is a characteristic (115), located within as an interior state (116 internal:ib-state). The absences: no seat (104 none) — the pity is not organ-lodged but a state of the ruler; no manner (108 none) — the tenderness is not otherwise qualified; and source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no traced origin, no degree, no narrowing, no separately recorded result, no fence. The finding is that power in this psalm is read from the inside out: the king's greatness is his pity, and the target is deliberately the lowest — the weak, the needy, the helpless — so that the mark of the interior is tenderness bent toward those with no claim of strength.
narratives.story: In this song about the ideal king, his greatness is measured not by his power but by his tenderness: he has pity on the weak and the needy. This pity is not a fleeting feeling; it is bound up with actually rescuing them and saving their lives — the mercy inside him is what drives the saving he does. It is a settled part of who he is as king. The text does not say where the feeling comes from, how intense it is, or track any separate result; it simply shows that real royal greatness bends toward the lowest and most helpless. The inside of good power, here, is compassion aimed at those who have no strength to claim it.

narratives.narrative: Here pity turns toward a ruined place: God's servants 'have pity (chanan) on her dust' — tender regard for the very rubble of Zion (101 sense). It is classed as disposition (102 type), a leaning of the heart rather than a bare deed. The bearer is the servants of God (105); the operation is to have pity or affection (106); the target is Zion's dust (107). Uniquely for this word here, the recorded coupling field carries the phrase internal:ib-state (112) and the locus field carries 'paired with holding her stones dear' (116) — the two are cross-lodged, but together they say the same thing: the pity is an interior state, welded to the parallel line where the servants hold her very stones dear. The discovery (114) reads it as the tender regard of the servants for ruined Zion, love for her very dust. It is a characteristic (115). The absences frame the tenderness: no seat (104 none) — not organ-lodged; no manner (108 none) — uncoloured; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no origin, degree, narrowing, result or fence. The finding worth marking is the target: pity here bends not toward a person but toward a place in ruins, even its dust and stones — the compassionate interior can be provoked by loss and rubble, loving what is broken because it is dear.
narratives.story: In this reading, pity is aimed at a ruined city. God's servants feel tenderness even for Zion's dust — they hold her broken stones dear and grieve over the rubble. It is a genuine leaning of the heart, not just an action, and it is knit together with that love for her stones. The text does not say where the feeling begins, how strong it is, or what it produces; it simply shows hearts moved by ruin. What is striking is that this compassion is stirred not by a suffering person but by a broken place — the caring heart can ache over wreckage and rubble, loving what is shattered simply because it matters to them.
narratives.variation_note: The two H2603:pity readings use the same verb (chanan) but run in opposite directions. Here (102:14) pity is present, active and warm — a disposition borne by God's servants toward ruined Zion, welded to holding her stones dear (an ascent). At 109:12 the same word appears only as a wished absence — 'nor any to pity his fatherless children' — with bearer 'no one', pity invoked precisely so that it be withheld (a descent). The difference in bearer (God's servants vs no one) and polarity (present tenderness vs curse-withheld mercy) is itself the finding: chanan can name both the heart that pities rubble and the heart that wills pity denied.

narratives.narrative: This reading fixes not on God's mercy directly but on the human image chosen to picture it: 'as a father shows compassion (racham) to his children' (101 sense). It is classed as disposition (102 type) — the settled tenderness of a parent's heart. The bearer named is a father (105) — the human father, whose pity is the analogy; the operation is to show compassion (106); the target is to his children (107). The recorded coupling field holds internal:ib-state (112) and the locus field holds 'paired with God's compassion on those who fear him' (116) — again cross-lodged, but together they mark it as an interior state set in parallel to the LORD's own compassion. The discovery (114) reads it precisely: the tender pity of a human father, the analogy for God's mercy. It is a characteristic (115). The inner-being lens matters here — though the verse's aim is God's mercy, the datum captured is the human father's compassion, the earthly interior scripture treats as the readable pattern of the divine. The absences: no seat (104 none) — the father's compassion is not organ-lodged; no manner (108 none) — uncoloured; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no origin, degree, narrowing, separate result or fence. The finding is that the deepest human tenderness — a father over his children — is taken as the very measure by which God's compassion is made intelligible, the inner life of the parent standing as the known term in the comparison.
narratives.story: This reading looks at the human picture used to explain God's mercy: a father's tenderness toward his children. The point of the verse is God's compassion, but what is actually captured here is the father's — the deep, settled softness of a parent's heart for his own, set right alongside the way the Lord cares for those who revere him. The text does not say where this fatherly feeling comes from, how strong it runs, or what it leads to; it simply holds it up. And that is the striking thing: the most tender thing we know in ordinary life, a parent bending over a child, is taken as the yardstick that makes God's mercy understandable.

narratives.narrative: In the great imprecatory psalm, pity appears only to be wished away: 'nor any to pity (chanan) his fatherless children' (101 sense). It is classed as disposition (102 type), the same tender leaning — but here named precisely so that it be denied. The bearer is 'no one' (105): the reading's spine is an absence deliberately willed, pity invoked as a thing that must find no one to carry it. The operation is pity (106); the target is the enemy's fatherless children (107). The recorded coupling holds internal:ib-state (112) and the locus holds 'paired with the kindness withheld' (116) — cross-lodged, but together binding this withheld pity to the withheld kindness of the same verse. The discovery (114) states it plainly: the wish that the pitiless find no pity for his own. This is the descent read at full weight (directive 5): the psalmist's interior here is not compassionate but retributive, and the data must be reported without softening — mercy is summoned as the exact thing to be refused to a man's children. It is still classed a characteristic (115). The absences sharpen it: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — the curse names no origin, degree, narrowing, result or fence, only the bare will that no pity come. The finding is that within this family the very word for tenderness can be turned as a weapon — the interior wishing that the merciless reap mercilessness, pity real enough to be pointedly denied.
narratives.story: In this bitter psalm of cursing, pity shows up only so that it can be refused. The psalmist wishes that no one — not a single person — would ever show kindness to his enemy's orphaned children. The tender feeling is named on purpose, precisely to be shut off, tied to the kindness he also wants withheld. This is the harsh side of the human heart shown without excuse: not softness here but a wish for payback, that a merciless man should himself find no mercy for his own. The text gives no reason, no measure, no outcome — just the bare will that pity be denied. It shows that even the word for tenderness can be swung like a weapon.
narratives.variation_note: This second H2603:pity reading inverts the first (102:14). Same verb chanan, same disposition-type, but the bearer collapses from God's servants to 'no one', and the polarity flips from present, warm regard for ruined Zion to a curse that pity be withheld from an enemy's children. The variation is the finding: the identical inner word runs as ascent (compassion given) at 102:14 and as descent (compassion willed absent) at 109:12 — how the tender interior can be turned into an instrument of retribution.

narratives.narrative: Beside the withheld pity of the same verse stands withheld kindness: 'Let there be none to extend kindness (chesed) to him' (101 sense). It is classed as disposition (102 type) — the settled loyal-love — but, like its neighbour, summoned only to be refused. The bearer is 'no one' (105): kindness is named as a thing the psalmist wills that nobody supply. The operation is to extend kindness (106); the target is the enemy (107). The recorded coupling holds internal:ib-state (112) and the locus holds 'paired with none to pity his children' (116) — cross-lodged, welding this refused chesed to the refused pity so that the two form a single imprecation. The discovery (114) names it: the wish that the merciless man find no mercy. This is chesed — the weightiest Hebrew word for steadfast covenant kindness — turned into the very thing the interior wants denied, and the data must stand uncomforted (directive 6). It is a characteristic (115). Preserve the distinction from the paired pity (directive 8): chesed here is loyal, extended kindness (the reaching hand of loyalty), pity is chanan (the softened heart) — the psalmist wills that both, hand and heart alike, come to his enemy from no one. The absences: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — only the naked wish that kindness find no bearer. The finding is that even steadfast covenant-kindness can be named inside a curse, invoked as the good the interior wants pointedly refused.
narratives.story: Right next to the wish that no one pity his enemy's children, the psalmist adds: let no one show him kindness either. This is the strongest word for loyal, faithful love — and it appears here only so it can be shut off. He wants nobody at all to extend it. The refused kindness and the refused pity go together as one dark wish. It is worth noticing the difference between them: kindness here is the loyal, reaching hand of steady love, while the pity beside it is the softened heart — and he wants both, hand and heart, to reach his enemy from no one. No reason is given, no measure, no result — just the bare desire that kindness find no one willing to give it. Even the noblest form of love can be named inside a curse.
narratives.variation_note: First of three H2617:kindnes readings, and the harshest. Here chesed is willed absent (bearer 'no one') toward an enemy — kindness named inside a curse. It differs from #2 (109:16), where the enemy himself is the one who failed to show kindness (bearer 'the enemy'; a diagnosis of his crime rather than a wish against him), and sharply from #3 (141:5), where kindness is received, not withheld — a rebuke welcomed as care. The arc across the three runs curse-withheld → accused-failure → embraced-correction; the shifting bearer (no one → the enemy → the psalmist) is the finding.

narratives.narrative: A few lines on, kindness returns as the measure of the enemy's guilt: 'he did not remember to show kindness (chesed)' (101 sense). It is classed as disposition (102 type). Now the bearer shifts decisively to the enemy himself (105): where at v12 kindness was willed absent by the psalmist, here its absence is diagnosed as the enemy's own crime. The operation is, precisely, to fail to show kindness (106) — the disposition read in the negative, as a settled omission; the target is the afflicted (107), for the passage adds that he pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted to put them to death. The recorded coupling holds internal:ib-state (112) and the locus holds 'paired with the failure to remember' (116) — cross-lodged, binding the failed kindness to the failure of memory: he did not remember to show it. The discovery (114) names it as the mercy the enemy withheld, the root of his condemnation. It is a characteristic (115). This is the descent read from the inside of the wicked man (directive 5): his guilt is located not first in his acts but in an interior that could not be bothered to recall kindness — mercilessness as forgetting. The absences: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — the failed kindness has no traced origin, degree, narrowing, separate result or fence. The finding is that kindness can be captured entirely by its lack, and that lack read as an inner failure of remembrance: the condemnable interior is the one for whom mercy simply never came to mind.
narratives.story: A little later the psalm names exactly what made the enemy guilty: he never remembered to be kind. Here the failure is his own — not something wished on him, but the real fault in him. Instead of showing mercy he hunted down the poor, the needy, and the broken-hearted to destroy them. His crime is traced back to something inside: kindness simply never crossed his mind. No cause is given, no measure, no separate outcome — just this settled blank where mercy should have been. The lesson is unsettling: a person can be condemned not only for cruel acts but for an inner life in which kindness was never even remembered.
narratives.variation_note: Second H2617:kindnes reading. It shares the negative polarity of #1 (109:12) — kindness in absence — but the bearer moves from 'no one' (a curse the psalmist wills) to 'the enemy' (a fault the enemy himself owns): here mercilessness is diagnosed, not invoked, and coupled to a failure of memory ('did not remember'). It is the mirror of #3 (141:5), where kindness is present and welcomed. The bearer-shift no one → the enemy, and the reframing from wished-curse to diagnosed-crime, is the finding.

narratives.narrative: In the portrait of the God-fearer, grace becomes a human trait: 'he is gracious (chanun), merciful, and righteous' (101 sense). It is classed as disposition (102 type) — a settled kindly bent. The bearer is the man, the one who fears the LORD (105); the operation is to be gracious (106); the target is others (107). The recorded coupling holds internal:ib-state (112) and the locus holds 'paired with being merciful and righteous' (116) — cross-lodged, welding graciousness into a triad with mercy and righteousness so that it is read not alone but as one facet of an integrated character. The discovery (114) states the theological weight lightly: the God-fearer mirrors God's own grace toward others — the same chanun spoken of God (103:8) now borne by the man. It is a characteristic (115). Preserve the distinction from its paired sister (directive 8): 'gracious' (chanun) is the disposition to bend favourably toward others; 'merciful' (rachum) beside it is the womb-deep compassion — two adjacent shades of the one merciful interior. The absences: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — the graciousness has no traced origin, no degree, no narrowing, no separate recorded result, no fence. The finding is that grace, which at 45:2 was the king's possessed charm and at 55:1 a favour begged of God, appears here as a moral disposition the ordinary righteous man carries toward his neighbours — grace become an outgoing kindness that images the God who is himself gracious.
narratives.story: In this picture of a person who reveres God, grace turns into a human character trait: he is gracious, merciful, and upright, all together. Grace here is a settled kindly leaning toward other people, one thread woven in with mercy and honesty into a whole good character. And the quiet point is that the very quality the psalms elsewhere say God has, this ordinary faithful person now carries — he mirrors it toward the people around him. The text does not say where it comes from in him, how strong it is, or what it produces; it simply names it. What is striking across the family is the shift: grace that was once a king's charm, or a favour begged from God, is here plain neighbourly kindness in an everyday good person.

narratives.narrative: Set immediately beside 'gracious' in the same verse, this reading names the God-fearer 'merciful (rachum)' (101 sense) — the womb-deep compassion, the tenderness of the innermost gut. It is classed as disposition (102 type). The bearer is the man (105); the operation is to be merciful (106); the target is others (107). The recorded coupling holds internal:ib-state (112) and the locus holds 'paired with being gracious' (116) — cross-lodged, welding rachum to chanun as its twin in the triad of v4. The discovery (114) reads it as the compassion of the God-fearer, God's mercy reflected in the man — rachum, elsewhere a signature word for the LORD (103:8), here borne by a human interior. It is a characteristic (115). The distinction from its paired sister must be kept (directive 8): where 'gracious' (chanun) is the favourable bending toward another, 'merciful' (rachum) is the deep visceral pity — the two are not collapsed but held as adjacent registers of the one compassionate character, disposition (favour) and disposition (gut-tenderness) side by side. The absences: no seat (104 none) — notably, though rachum is etymologically the word of the womb, no bodily seat is recorded here, the compassion read as a whole-person state rather than organ-lodged; no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent. The finding is that the God-fearer's interior is described in the very vocabulary of God's own mercy, and that within one verse two shades of that mercy — the gracious bend and the visceral tenderness — are held distinct yet fused.
narratives.story: In the same breath that calls the God-fearer gracious, the psalm also calls him merciful — a word that reaches down to the deepest, gut-level tenderness. It is a settled part of who he is, aimed at other people, and it stands paired with his graciousness as its close twin. These two are not the same: being gracious is bending kindly toward someone, while being merciful is that deep inward ache of pity — and the verse keeps both, side by side. Strikingly, though this word for mercy originally pictures the womb, the text lodges it in no single part of him; it is the whole person. And once again the quality is the very one the psalms use for God himself, now living in a human heart.

narratives.narrative: The next verse turns the God-fearer's grace into transaction: 'it is well with the man who deals generously (chanan) and lends' (101 sense). Notably the same root chanan that elsewhere in this family means 'pity' is here read as open-handed generosity — grace enacted in the lending of goods. It is classed as action (102 type), not merely a bent but a deed done. The bearer is the man (105); the operation is to deal generously (106); the target is 'and lend' (107) — the generosity spilling directly into concrete lending. The recorded coupling holds internal:ib-state (112) and the locus holds 'paired with conducting affairs with justice' (116) — cross-lodged, binding generous dealing to just conduct, so that open-handedness and fair management are one practice. The discovery (114) names it as the open-handed generosity of the God-fearer. It is a characteristic (115). Preserve the distinction (directive 8): where v4's 'gracious/merciful' were dispositions (102 type disposition), this v5 item is an action (102 type action) — the same interior grace now moving out into economic practice, feeling become deed. The absences: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no origin, degree, narrowing, separate result or fence. The finding is that the grace which was disposition in v4 becomes, in v5, transaction: the merciful heart of the God-fearer is shown to work itself out in how he handles money — lending freely and running his affairs justly — so that the inner mercy is verified at the level of goods.
narratives.story: The very next line shows the God-fearer's kindness at work in ordinary business: he deals generously and lends. Interestingly, the same root word that elsewhere means 'to pity' here means open-handed giving — mercy turned into practical generosity with money and goods. This is not just a feeling now but something he does, and it goes hand in hand with running his affairs fairly. Where the line before described his kind and tender character, this line shows that character in action, spending itself in how he lends and manages what he has. The text gives no cause, measure, or further outcome — it simply shows a merciful heart proved true at the level of everyday dealings.

narratives.narrative: This reading catches the plea for mercy at the moment it is answered: 'he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy (tachanun)' (101 sense). It is classed as action (102 type) — the supplication the interior performs. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to plead for mercy (106); the target is God (107). The coupling holds external:god (112): the plea reaches wholly outside the self toward God, and its locus too is 'paired with the love and calling' (116) — for the psalm opens 'I love the LORD, because he has heard.' The discovery (114) reads it as the supplications God heard, the cry that drew forth love. It is a characteristic (115). The distinctive note is retrospective gratitude: unlike the raw begging of 55:1, here the plea is remembered as already heard, and the interior's answering movement is love — the supplication that was met now generating affection for the God who inclined his ear. The absences: no seat (104 none) — the plea is the whole self reaching, not organ-lodged; no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no traced origin, degree, narrowing, separately recorded result or fence. The finding is that the plea for mercy is read here not in its distress but in its aftermath: mercy asked and mercy granted, the humbled cry closing the loop into love, so that supplication is shown as the doorway through which affection for God enters the interior.
narratives.story: This reading catches the cry for mercy after it has been answered. The psalmist begins, 'I love the Lord, because he has heard my voice and my pleas' — so the plea is remembered as one that was already granted. It is something he did, reaching out entirely toward God. And the response inside him is love: because God bent down to listen, affection wells up. Unlike a raw cry of distress, this looks back with gratitude. The text does not say where the plea began in him, how loud it was, or track a separate result; it simply shows that asking for mercy and receiving it opened a door — and through that door love for God came in.
narratives.variation_note: First of three H8469:pleasformercy readings. This one is retrospective and grateful — the plea remembered as heard, its coupling to God (external:god) and its pairing with love and calling marking it as answered supplication that generates affection. It differs from #2 (130:2), a present cry 'out of the depths' still awaiting answer, and from #3 (140:6), where the plea is classed not as action but as affect and coupled to the voice itself (voice-pleas, internal) as a counter-move against schemers. The shift from answered-and-loved → depth-cry-hoping → embattled-vocal-appeal is the finding.

narratives.narrative: Here the plea for mercy rises still unanswered, out of the depths: 'let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy (tachanun)' (101 sense). It is classed as action (102 type) — the supplication the interior lifts. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is to plead for mercy (106); the target is God (107, 'before God'). The coupling holds external:god (112), and the locus is 'paired with the cry' (116) — for v1 is 'out of the depths I cry to you.' The discovery (114) reads it as the supplication, the cry sharpened into a plea for grace. It is a characteristic (115). The distinctive weight here is the position: this plea is voiced from the depths, before any hearing, in a psalm that goes on to reason 'if you should mark iniquities, who could stand? but with you there is forgiveness' — so the plea is grounded in the confessed impossibility of standing on merit. The absences: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no traced origin, degree, narrowing, separate result or fence recorded. The finding is that the plea for mercy is here the interior at its lowest reach, crying upward from the depths with no claim of its own — supplication as the only posture left to one who knows that if sins were counted he could not stand, and who casts himself entirely on the forgiveness that is with God.
narratives.story: Here the cry for mercy is still going up, unanswered, from the very bottom: 'out of the depths I cry to you — let your ears hear my pleas.' It is something the psalmist is doing, reaching out toward God from as low as a person can be. And the plea rests on a stark admission that comes next in the psalm: if God kept score of sins, no one could survive it — but there is forgiveness with him. So this is the cry of someone who knows he has no claim of his own and throws himself entirely on God's mercy. The text names no source, no measure, no result — just a soul at its lowest, calling upward, with nothing to stand on but grace.
narratives.variation_note: Second H8469:pleasformercy reading. Like #1 (116:1) it is classed as action and coupled to God (external:god), but where #1 looks back on the plea as already heard (and answered with love), this one is a present, unanswered cry 'out of the depths,' grounded in the confession that no one could stand if sins were marked. It differs more sharply from #3 (140:6), classed as affect and coupled to the voice (voice-pleas) as a counter-move against schemers. The variation — answered-gratitude vs depth-cry-in-hope vs embattled-appeal — tracks the same word across relief, need, and threat.

narratives.narrative: In a psalm ringed by violent schemers, the plea for mercy becomes the interior's vocal counter-move: 'give ear to the voice of my pleas for mercy' — pleas voiced (101 sense). Uniquely among the three, it is classed not as action but as affect (102 type) — read as an inner emotional surge sounded outward rather than a bare performed act. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is expansive: the psalmist lifts a crying voice of supplication, the cry as the counter-move to the schemes (106); the target is 'crying-out' itself (107). The coupling is 'voice-pleas' (112) — note the shift: where #1 and #2 coupled the plea externally to God, here the coupling binds the plea to the voice that carries it, and the locus returns to internal:ib-state (116). The discovery (114) reads it precisely: against the silent scheming, the psalmist's interior goes vocal, appealing upward. It is a characteristic (115). The finding lies in the contrast the passage sets up: the wicked plan evil in the heart, make their tongue sharp as a serpent's, hide traps in silence — and against all that hidden, venomous quiet the psalmist's one weapon is a raised, pleading voice. The absences: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no origin, degree, narrowing, separate result or fence. So supplication here is the interior's answer to menace: not a scheme met with a scheme but silence met with an open, upward cry for mercy.
narratives.story: In this psalm the enemies work in silence — plotting evil in their hearts, sharpening their tongues like snakes, hiding traps along the path. Against all that quiet menace, the psalmist has one response: he raises his voice and pleads for mercy. Here the cry is felt as much as done — an emotional surge sounded out loud — and it is tied to the very voice that carries it, an appeal thrown upward. He does not answer scheming with scheming; he answers hidden threats with an open, pleading cry. The text names no cause, measure, or outcome for it. What it shows is a person who, when surrounded and endangered, meets the silence of his enemies by crying out for mercy.
narratives.variation_note: Third H8469:pleasformercy reading, and the most distinct. It alone is classed as affect (not action, as #1 116:1 and #2 130:2), and it alone couples the plea to the voice that carries it (voice-pleas) with an internal locus, rather than externally to God. Its sense wording is 'pleas voiced' and its setting is embattlement — the cry as counter-move against silent schemers — where #1 is answered gratitude and #2 a depth-cry in hope. The three together show the same supplication running across relief, need, and threat, shifting from a God-directed act to an inwardly-felt vocal surge; the type-shift (action → affect) and coupling-shift (external:god → voice-pleas) is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The last kindness in the family is the strangest and the finding-richest: a blow received as love. 'Let a righteous man strike me — it is a kindness; let him rebuke me — it is oil for my head' — rebuke received as kindness (101 sense). Uniquely it is classed as affect (102 type), an inner reception rather than a deed or a bare disposition. The bearer is the psalmist (105), and here he is the receiver, not the giver, of kindness. The operation is fully drawn: a righteous man's blow or rebuke is welcomed as kindness, oil for the head — correction embraced (106); the target is 'embrace-correction' (107). The coupling is 'rebuke-is-kindness' (112) — the astonishing equation itself, the strike welded to the word kindness — and the locus is internal:ib-state (116). The discovery (114) marks how rare this is: the operation is rare: the interior wants to be corrected, receiving reproof as care. It is a characteristic (115). The finding is precisely this inversion: kindness elsewhere in the family is a gift the giver extends outward; here it is a gift the receiver recognises in what feels like an assault, the interior so ordered that it reads a righteous rebuke as oil, not injury, and welcomes the wound. The absences: no seat (104 none); no manner (108 none); source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent — no traced origin, degree, narrowing, separate result or fence. Against the enemies of the surrounding verses, whose delicacies the psalmist refuses, this is an interior that would rather take a good man's blow than a wicked man's dainties — kindness discerned from the receiving end, in the very thing that hurts.
narratives.story: The last and most surprising kindness in this group is a blow taken as love. The psalmist says: let a good man strike me — that is a kindness; let him correct me — it is like soothing oil on my head; I will not refuse it. Here kindness is not something he gives but something he receives, and he finds it in what feels like an attack. His inner life is so well-ordered that he welcomes an honest rebuke as care rather than injury, and even embraces the sting. Surrounded by tempting, corrupt company whose delicacies he turns down, he would rather take a good man's hard words than a bad man's treats. The text gives no cause or measure — just a heart that recognizes love in correction and gladly takes the wound.
narratives.variation_note: Third and final H2617:kindnes reading, and the polar opposite of the other two. Where #1 (109:12) wills kindness withheld (bearer 'no one') and #2 (109:16) diagnoses the enemy's failure to show it (bearer 'the enemy'), here kindness is present and welcomed — and the bearer is the psalmist as receiver, not giver. It alone is classed affect (vs disposition in #1 and #2) and alone runs as an ascent. The identical word chesed thus spans a curse-withheld, an accused-failure, and an embraced rebuke; the movement of the bearer (no one → the enemy → the psalmist-as-receiver) and of polarity (denied → failed → welcomed) is the finding.
